facts.one_liner: Midway Geyser Basin’s Grand Prismatic—rainbow rings of thermophiles around Yellowstone’s largest hot spring.
facts.why_go: The hero photo is Grand Prismatic Spring and Midway Geyser Basin from above: a deep blue center ringed by yellow, orange, and rusty microbial mats, with steam drifting over boardwalks and the Firehole River corridor. NPS notes Grand Prismatic is Yellowstone’s largest hot spring—roughly 200–330 feet across and more than 121 feet deep—colored by heat-loving thermophiles that grade from colorless and yellow in the hottest water to orange, brown, and green in cooler margins. From the Fairy Falls parking area, the Grand Prismatic Overlook Trail climbs about 105 feet over 0.6 miles for the classic aerial-style view that matches this image; the Midway boardwalks put you at spring level. Stay on boardwalks—hydrothermal water can cause severe burns.
facts.best_time: Late spring through early fall when park roads to Midway are open to regular vehicles (West Entrance–Madison typically mid-April through late October; confirm NPS road dates). Early morning for lighter parking and clearer steam views; midsummer midday can haze boardwalk views with steam.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into West Yellowstone (seasonal), Bozeman, Jackson, Cody, Billings, or Idaho Falls, then drive. Midway Geyser Basin sits on the Grand Loop between Madison and Old Faithful—about 30 minutes West Entrance to Madison, then south toward Old Faithful. Park at Midway for boardwalks or ~1 mile south at Fairy Falls for the overlook trail; parking is very limited 10 am–6 pm.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable U.S. national park; entrance pass required (no prices listed here). No timed entry for Midway itself. Remain on boardwalks and designated trails; supervise children. Check NPS Current Conditions and road status before travel—seasonal closures and temporary trail restrictions can affect Fairy Falls beyond the overlook.

facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable; park entrance fee/pass required (no prices listed). Yosemite is not using a season-wide timed entry reservation system in 2026—expect active traffic and parking management instead. Overlook is wheelchair accessible from designated parking.

facts.why_go: The hero photo shows Moraine Lake thawing in spring: broken ice floes on still turquoise water beneath the jagged Ten Peaks, with rock rubble and sparse shoreline trees—not a midsummer crowded dock scene. Glacial silt (rock flour) suspended in meltwater scatters light to create the lake’s trademark blue-green when ice unlocks. Parks Canada treats Moraine Lake as a backcountry lakeshore destination: Moraine Lake Road is closed year-round to personal vehicles, with access by reserved Parks Canada shuttle, licensed commercial operators, or Moraine Lake Lodge guests. The classic rockpile shoreline and canoe dock area frame the Ten Peaks backdrop once the ice goes out.
facts.best_time: Parks Canada Moraine Lake shuttle season for 2026: June 1–October 12 (weather permitting)—prime for open water and peak turquoise. Early season (soon after ice-out) matches the thawing photo mood; midsummer is busiest. Lake Louise Lakeshore shuttles start earlier (May 15).
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Calgary (YYC), drive Trans-Canada Highway to Banff/Lake Louise. Check in at the Lake Louise Park and Ride (Lake Louise Ski Resort / 1 Whitehorn Road) for reserved Parks Canada shuttles to Moraine Lake; Roam transit and licensed operators also serve the area. Do not plan to drive a private car to the Moraine parking lot.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable national park; Parks Canada entry pass plus a separate shuttle (or licensed operator) reservation are required for most visitors—no prices listed here. Moraine has pit toilets only—no cell service, Wi‑Fi, running water, or lighting. Book shuttle seats early; seats typically sell out.

facts.one_liner: Maligne Lake—largest natural lake in the Canadian Rockies, ringed by snow-capped peaks.
facts.why_go: The hero photo is Maligne Lake itself: a long, glacier-fed expanse of deep blue water framed by forested shores and snow-and-ice-capped mountains—the classic Jasper alpine-lake vista. Parks Canada calls Maligne the largest natural lake in the Canadian Rockies, about 22 km long, stretching past Spirit Island toward Coronet Glacier melt channels. Lodgepole pine and spruce around the north end shelter moose, Harlequin ducks, and other wildlife. Spirit Island—one of the Rockies’ most photographed islets—lies about 14 km up-lake with no road or trail access; tour boats or private non-motorized craft are the only ways to reach it, while the lakeshore day-use area matches the open water-and-peaks composition in the photo.
facts.best_time: Late May through mid-October for road access, boat cruises, and paddling; summer for fullest services. Winter brings cross-country skiing on Maligne Valley trails when conditions allow. Early morning for calm water reflections and wildlife along Maligne Lake Road.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Jasper townsite. Drive Highway 16 east briefly, then Maligne Lake Road about 48 km to the lakeshore (allow ~1–1.5 hours for wildlife delays and parking). Fly into Edmonton (YEG) or Calgary (YYC) and continue by road; seasonal rail and coach options serve Jasper. Boat cruises and rentals operate seasonally from the historic boathouse area.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable; Parks Canada entry pass required for adults (youth admission policies apply—confirm current rules; no prices listed). Watch for wildlife jams on Maligne Lake Road. Boat cruise tickets are separate from park entry. Stay overnight in Jasper; day-use parking at the lake fills in peak season.

facts.one_liner: Los Cuernos del Paine—horn peaks with dark sedimentary caps over pale granite above Patagonian lakes.

CONAF describes the Paine massif as an independent mountain system shaped by glacial advance and retreat, with sedimentary rock high and granite below—the geologic recipe behind the Cuernos’ banded look. The park (created 1959; UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1978) pairs those horns with guanaco steppe, lenga forest, and icefields fed by the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. Day visitors and W-circuit hikers see the Cuernos from lakeshores and trail segments toward Refugio Los Cuernos and Valle Francés.
facts.best_time: Southern Hemisphere summer (roughly December–February) for longest daylight and fullest trail services; shoulder months (Oct–Nov, Mar–Apr) for fewer crowds and changeable weather. Winter visits are possible on authorized routes with winter protocols—confirm CONAF notices. Circuito Macizo Paine (O circuit) noted closed into late 2026 on CONAF channels—verify before booking multi-day treks.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Punta Arenas, bus or drive to Puerto Natales (~250 km paved), then continue ~80–150 km to park gates (Laguna Amarga, Sarmiento, or Serrano approaches). Regular buses from Puerto Natales typically leave morning and early afternoon toward Laguna Amarga / Pudeto / administration. Buy entrance passes via Chile’s official Pases Parques system in advance.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable national park; ticketed entry via Pases Parques (buy ahead—no prices listed). Overnight W/O trekking requires confirmed campsite/refuge reservations with authorized operators. Strict fire and camping rules; no drones without special authorization. Strong Patagonian wind year-round—pack layers.

facts.one_liner: Argentina-side Iguazú Falls—jungle-framed cataracts and boardwalk circuits in Parque Nacional Iguazú.
facts.why_go: The hero photo is the Argentine side of Iguazú Falls: multiple horseshoe curtains of white water plunging into mist below subtropical Selva Paranaense canopy—the view from Área Cataratas walkways rather than a Brazilian panorama. Argentina’s Parque Nacional Iguazú (created 1934; UNESCO World Heritage 1984) protects more than 67,000 hectares of Atlantic Forest ecoregion around the falls on the border with Brazil. Ticketed circuits include the Upper Circuit (panoramic tops of the falls), Lower Circuit (closer spray and stairs sections), and Garganta del Diablo (Devil’s Throat) reached via the Ecological Train of the Jungle. The Argentine boardwalks weave among dozens of individual drops, matching the layered falls-through-forest composition in the photo.
facts.best_time: Year-round; park open every day including holidays. Shoulder seasons (roughly Apr–Jun, Aug–Sep) often balance flow and humidity; summer is hotter and wetter with fuller spray. Morning entry time slots help beat heat and crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Cataratas del Iguazú Airport (IGR) near Puerto Iguazú, or cross from Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, with valid border documents. Buses from Puerto Iguazú terminal (Río Uruguay line) run frequently to Ruta Nacional 101 Km 142 Área Cataratas. On-site parking is available at the portal; tickets for general entry are sold online and at boletería.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable; ticketed national park (entry includes open circuits and Ecological Train—no prices listed). Respect the time window on your ticket. General Área Cataratas hours typically 8:00–18:00 (last entry 16:00); extended hours on some peak dates. Insect repellent recommended; no pets inside. facts.why_go: The hero photo matches Plitvice’s signature scene: stepped turquoise-to-emerald lakes cascading over living tufa barriers and waterfalls between forested shores. UNESCO and the park explain that calcium carbonate deposition—helped by mosses, algae, and bacteria—builds porous travertine (tufa) dams that continually reshape 16 named lakes in Upper and Lower groups. Park interpreters note Lower Lakes canyon walks often show surreal turquoise and deep-blue tones, while forest-wrapped Upper Lakes lean emerald green depending on light, depth, and dissolved matter. Wooden boardwalks, an electric boat on Kozjak, and a panoramic train stitch the viewpoints that produce this postcard composition.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for strong color, active waterfalls, and fewer peak-summer crowds. Arrive at your booked morning slot or later afternoon. Winter: Lower Lakes usually open; Upper Lakes often closed until roughly early April depending on weather.

Stay on marked paths to protect fragile tufa.
